title: Nigerians Must Obtain Tax ID To Operate Bank Accounts By 2026 - New Tax Law - Business - Nigeria
content: The Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025, signed by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, will take effect on 1 January 2026. From that date, no individual or business can open or operate a bank account, run a business, or access financial services without a Taxpayer Identification Number (TIN). The law also requires all government agencies (MDAs) and foreign suppliers to obtain a TIN before entering contracts or doing business in Nigeria. Under Section 8(2), banks, insurers, and stockbrokers will be barred from providing services to anyone without a valid TIN. The reform is described as the most significant change in Nigeria’s financial and tax system in decades, aiming to widen the tax net and reduce reliance on oil. Key metrics cited in the article include Nigeria’s 10 % tax‑to‑GDP ratio compared with Ghana’s 13 %, Kenya’s 16 %, South Africa’s 27 %+, and the global average of 34 %. Out of over 200 million citizens, only 10 million are registered taxpayers, while more than 60 million Nigerians hold bank accounts. The Act also abolishes the Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS) and replaces it with the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS). Public reactions quoted a civil servant in Abuja saying, 'It's good for accountability, but I fear delays and corruption in the process,' and a Lagos‑based tax consultant who welcomed the reform, stating, 'This is long overdue. Without linking tax IDs to financial services, compliance will never improve.' The article notes potential risks such as exclusion of the 38 million unbanked adults, bureaucratic delays, corruption, and an awareness gap that could create chaos at tax offices.

title: Nigerian banks eye finishing line on recapitalisation - MyJoyOnline
content:
Nigerian banks face a March 26 2026 deadline to meet new capital requirements set by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN). In March 2024 the regulator gave banks two years to raise the minimum capital: 500 bn naira for banks with local and international operations, 200 bn naira for national‑only banks, 50 bn naira for regional and merchant banks, 20 bn naira for non‑interest national banks and 10 bn naira for non‑interest regional banks. This is the first capital‑raising mandate in two decades, the last being in 2004 when the cap was 25 bn naira.

Only eight of the 26 banks have met the targets. Access Bank reached 595 bn naira, Zenith Bank 615 bn naira, Ecobank Nigeria and Jaiz Bank already met their thresholds, and Guaranty Trust Bank raised 351 bn naira through a rights issue and $105 m on the London Stock Exchange. United Bank for Africa (UBA) has raised 251 bn naira and plans to finish its capital‑raising by the end of Q3, while First Bank’s progress is stalled by a takeover battle.

Fitch Ratings notes that "Strong investor appetite has ensured that the vast majority of capital raisings so far have been successful," and that most first‑ and second‑tier banks should meet the new requirements through capital raisings alone, reducing the likelihood of sector consolidation.

Second‑tier banks Fidelity and FCMB have raised 176 bn naira and are pursuing additional private placements. Wema Bank, after a 50 bn naira private placement, expects a 276 bn naira capital base, 34 % above the required 200 bn naira.

Some banks are opting for mergers: Union Bank and Titan Trust Bank have merged, and Unity Bank and Providus Bank plan to merge to secure a national licence. Standard Chartered’s local bank holds 45.4 bn naira and needs 154 bn naira more; Citibank’s local bank has 14.4 bn naira and needs 185 bn naira. Both banks can raise funds, merge, or exit Nigeria.

CBN governor Olayemi Cardoso said at a July monetary policy briefing that "There has been a lot of interest locally in investing in the banks," and that the bank will "continue to do our part by building resilience, creating buffers and adhering to the rules."

title: Financial literacy, innovation take centre stage in Nigeria’s financial inclusion drive - Businessday NG
content: Businessday NG reports that Nigeria aims for 80 % financial inclusion by 2030, a goal that requires deeper financial literacy, product innovation and evidence‑based policy. At the Access to Financial Services (A2F) 2025 stakeholder event, panelists compared Nigeria’s journey to the 2008 crisis, noting that lack of awareness can cripple economies. Kalu Aja, Lead at Kalu Aja LLC, said 'Alan Greenspan once said that lack of financial planning was the biggest problem facing the world, even bigger than wars,' stressing that literacy is urgent. The A2F survey, a biannual, nationally representative demand‑side survey by EFInA, interviewed more than 27 000 Nigerians across 1 800 communities and covers all 36 states and the FCT. Recent data show digital payments rose from 34 % in 2020 to 45 % in 2023, yet credit access remains below 5 %, pensions have not grown beyond formal workers and mobile banking adoption is under 50 %. Fintech leaders admit innovation has focused on payments, with credit, insurance and pensions lagging, but momentum is shifting. Ajibade Laolu‑Adewale, Chairman of CeBIH, said 'Once payments worked, unicorns emerged, and investors came in,' and added that integrating payments with pensions and insurance will win the market. The 2025 A2F edition will add modules on consumer protection, financial literacy and women’s economic empowerment, and will measure financial literacy nationwide in partnership with the Central Bank of Nigeria. States such as Kaduna already use A2F data to shape policy. EFInA CEO Foyinsolami Akinjayeju emphasized that the survey’s value lies in post‑survey action: 'The goal of a survey is really what happens after the survey. We want to ensure that whatever innovations we are introducing align with you, the policymakers, providers, and regulators. That way, the results remain relevant and actionable,' she said. Research Associate Chioma Nwaiwu noted that the 2025 survey will help states design targeted interventions amid inflation and cost‑of‑living pressures: 'With inflation, food insecurity, and cost‑of‑living pressures squeezing households, the 2025 survey will play a critical role in identifying gaps and informing both national and state‑level policies,' she said.

title: Banks' total assets to reach N242.3trn by December 2025 - Agusto & Co.
content: According to a 2025 Nigerian Banking industry report by Agusto & Co., total banking assets are projected to reach N242.3 trillion (≈$151.4 billion at N1,600/$) by 31 December 2025, up 44.9 % year‑on‑year from N186.6 trillion at 31 December 2024. The sector maintained a 59.4 % liquidity ratio at the end of 2024, compared with 43.5 % in FY 2023, and the agency expects the ratio to exceed 6 % by year‑end 2025. Commercial paper issuances rose to about N750 billion in the first seven months of 2025, signalling a shift toward innovative funding. In response to the Central Bank of Nigeria’s March 2024 directive on minimum paid‑up capital, 16 banks raised roughly N1.7 trillion in 2024, with an additional N800 billion secured in the first seven months of 2025; by 31 July 2025, eight banks had met the new capital requirement. Non‑performing loans climbed to 5.2 % of total industry loans as of 31 December 2024 (from 4.0 % FY 2023), and Agusto & Co. projects a short‑term rise to 6.9 % in 2025 as forbearance is withdrawn. Profitability is expected to dip in FY 2025, with a 19.2 % decline in profit before tax and a pre‑tax return on average equity falling to 27 % from 48.2 % in FY 2024, but the report maintains a ‘stable’ outlook, forecasting a rebound in FY 2026 as capital is deployed and impairment charges subside. The report notes, ‘Innovative funding strategies are becoming increasingly critical,’ and that ‘Capital raising activities will also help resolve breaches of the single obligor limit and support asset quality improvements.’

title: Using an ATM in Nigeria? Here's What is Changing Under CBN's New 2025 Guidelines | Pulse Nigeria
content: The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) introduced new ATM guidelines effective October 9, 2025, replacing the 2020 regulations and building on powers from the 2007 Act. The update aims to improve reliability, safety, and inclusivity in electronic banking across Nigeria. Key changes include a maximum 72-hour downtime for ATMs due to technical faults, with mandatory customer notification if longer. Banks and independent ATM deployers must ensure regular cash restocking, especially on weekends and holidays, and must not load unfit notes or allow ATMs to run without backup power. Refunds for failed transactions must now be processed within two days, a significant improvement over previous timelines that often stretched to weeks. The CBN mandates that at least 2% of all deployed ATMs include tactile symbols for visually impaired users and must be publicly listed on bank websites. All ATMs must have proper lighting, privacy features, secure locations, and anti-skimming devices. Hidden cameras must record transactions (excluding PIN entry), and transactions are automatically aborted if a user blocks the camera. Banks must display active helpline numbers at every ATM, maintain detailed ATM registers (including locations, serial numbers, and service records), and insure cash inside machines to protect against theft or vandalism. The CBN will enforce compliance through regular audits and onsite inspections, with penalties for non-compliance. These reforms follow the March 2024 circular focused on increasing bank capital requirements, but the October 2025 guidelines are broader, emphasizing security, accountability, and user experience. The changes are expected to restore confidence in electronic banking, particularly in a cash-dependent economy.

title: Cash outside banks shrinks to N4.45tn
content: Cash held outside the banking system in Nigeria fell to N4.45tn in August 2025, the lowest level recorded that year, according to the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) Money and Credit Statistics. This marked a decline of N41.1bn (0.9%) from June 2025 and N180bn (3.9%) from the year’s peak of N4.63tn in May 2025. Total currency in circulation reached N4.92tn in August, meaning 90.5% of all issued cash was outside banks. The trend shows persistent fluctuations but consistently high ratios: in January 2025, N4.74tn (90.5%) was outside banks, with monthly highs and lows throughout the year. On a year-on-year basis, cash outside banks rose from N3.87tn in August 2024 to N4.45tn in August 2025—a gain of N585bn (15.1%). Currency in circulation also increased from N4.14tn to N4.92tn (N778bn, 18.8%). Monthly comparisons show 2025 consistently outpaced 2024 by at least N585bn, with gaps reaching over N1.4tn in some months. Although the ratio of cash outside banks to total circulation was slightly lower in August 2025 (90.5%) compared to August 2024 (93.3%), the absolute value was significantly higher. The average stock of cash outside banks from January to August 2025 was N4.57tn, nearly N1.55tn above the N3.62tn average for the same period in 2024. This indicates that while the CBN has marginally reduced the proportion of cash outside banks, the overall base has expanded. The decline in August may reflect early effects of tighter cash management and growing digital payment adoption. However, over nine in ten naira in circulation remain outside banks. In September 2025, the CBN reduced the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) from 27.50% to 27%, citing easing inflation (20.12% in August) and the need to stimulate growth. The Cash Reserve Ratio for commercial banks was lowered from 50% to 45%, while the reserve ratio for public sector deposits was raised to 75%. The CBN also expressed concern about excess liquidity from Federation Account Allocation Committee (FAAC) disbursements, warning they could undermine disinflation and exchange rate stability. Governor Olayemi Cardoso stated, 'We are a bit concerned about excess liquidity... and we will continue to deploy the tools required to ensure that the stability we have attained stays with us into the future.' This rate cut aligns with broader African trends, as Ghana reduced its policy rate by 350 basis points to 21.5% and Kenya cut its benchmark rate to 9.5% in mid-August.

title: Recapitalisation: With 200 Days to Deadline, Banks Intensify Efforts to Scale Hurdle - THISDAYLIVE
content: With 200 days remaining until the Central Bank of Nigeria's March 31, 2026 recapitalisation deadline, Nigerian banks are accelerating capital‑raising efforts. The required capital gap was estimated at about $4.1 trillion; banks have so far raised $2.8 trillion. New thresholds set by the CBN are N500 billion for international banks, N200 billion for national banks, and N50 billion for regional banks. Eleven banks – Access Holdings, Zenith Bank, GTBank, Ecobank, Stanbic IBTC, Wema Bank, Jaiz Bank, Lotus Bank, Providus Bank, Greenwich Merchant Bank, and Premium Trust Bank – have already met their respective requirements. GTBank lifted its paid‑up capital from N138 billion to N504 billion after a N365.85 billion injection from its parent GTCO. Access and Zenith secured their positions through rights issues and public offers. Other institutions are pursuing rights issues, private placements, or asset sales; UBA is mid‑rights issue, Fidelity has raised more than N273 billion, FCMB raised N144.6 billion, and FSDH sold its stake in PAL Pensions. Nova Bank opted to remain regional, limiting its requirement to N50 billion, while Providus Bank is acquiring Unity Bank to move from regional to national status. Analysts say the programme is progressing smoothly. Ayokunle Olubunmi of Agusto & Co noted: 'Most are moving in line with their capital plans, and many are even ahead of schedule. Encouragingly, most of the funds have come from Nigerians, not foreign investors. Out of the roughly N4 trillion required, about N3 trillion has already been raised, largely from domestic investors.' A report by SBM Intelligence highlighted that the drive will reshape competition and support a $1 trillion economy. McKinsey’s Mayowa Kuyoro said the recapitalisation will enable institutions to grow and innovate, while Frederick Twum warned that consolidation and digital disruption will drive a new era of innovation.

title: How to make your bank account work across borders
content: The article explains how Nigerians can make their bank accounts work across borders by using a range of modern financial tools. It highlights four main strategies: (1) opening a domiciliary account, which lets users hold and transact in major currencies such as U.S. dollars, pounds sterling, or euros without converting to naira until the rate is favourable; (2) obtaining a multi‑currency debit or prepaid card that allows direct spending in foreign currencies for travel and online shopping; (3) using integrated international money‑transfer services (e.g., Western Union, MoneyGram, WorldRemit) that are now offered through Nigerian banks’ branches, ATMs and mobile apps, speeding up transfers and improving security; and (4) adopting fintech‑based digital wallets and virtual accounts from platforms such as Payoneer, Grey, Chipper Cash and Flutterwave, which provide foreign bank accounts and lower‑cost cross‑border payments. The piece also warns about hidden fees—banks may charge $10–$20 per domiciliary transfer and add exchange‑rate mark‑ups that erode value—and urges readers to compare costs and monitor rates. Finally, it stresses the importance of staying informed about Central Bank of Nigeria policy changes that can restrict naira debit cards or alter official and parallel market rates, which can disrupt international transactions. The article concludes that choosing the right mix of tools—domiciliary accounts for exporters, multi‑currency cards for travellers, and fintech wallets for freelancers—offers Nigerians greater control and flexibility in a global economy.

title: Non-TSA public accounts safe, accessible after 75% CRR - CBN - Businessday NG
content: The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) confirmed that funds in non-Treasury Single Account (non-TSA) public sector accounts remain safe and fully accessible at commercial banks, despite the introduction of a 75% Cash Reserve Requirement (CRR) on these deposits at its last Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting. The CBN stated that commercial banks have internal liquidity mechanisms and access to the Standing Lending Facility (SLF) as a lender of last resort to meet customer obligations. The 75% CRR was implemented to curb excess liquidity in the banking system and prevent inflationary pressures that could disrupt the ongoing disinflation trend. The MPC also reduced the Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) by 50 basis points to 27.00%, citing five consecutive months of declining inflation and expectations of further moderation through 2025. The Standing Facilities Corridor was adjusted from +500/-100 to +250/-250 basis points around the MPR to create a symmetric corridor, aiming to reduce overnight interest rate volatility, improve interbank market efficiency, and enhance monetary policy transmission. Additionally, the CRR for commercial banks was lowered to 45% to ease liquidity constraints and support productive lending, including to micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), while maintaining inflation control. Headline inflation fell to 20.12% in August 2025 from 21.88% in July, marking the fifth consecutive monthly decline and the sharpest drop in five months, driven by exchange rate stability, a current account surplus, falling petrol prices, and tight monetary policy. Experts project continued disinflation through 2025, supported by harvest season onset. The CBN emphasized that Nigeria’s external reserves remain strong, standing at $43.05 billion as of September 11, 2025, providing 8.28 months of import cover.
